paragraphs.heading: What the ISS is
paragraphs.text: The International Space Station, or ISS, is a space station circling Earth in low Earth orbit. Five space agencies run it together: NASA for the United States, Roscosmos for Russia, ESA for Europe, JAXA for Japan and CSA for Canada. It was the first station built, kept up and crewed by nations working together, and it is the largest spacecraft for people ever made. It works as a research station, where scientists run experiments in microgravity and study the space environment.

paragraphs.heading: Size and orbit
paragraphs.text: The station flies about 400 kilometres up, beneath most space debris and the Van Allen radiation belts, and its path ranges between 51.64° north and south. It travels at 7.67 km/s and goes around Earth roughly every 93 minutes, about 15.5 times a day. With its solar arrays it spans 109 m by 73 m, about the size of a football field. The space inside that is kept under pressure is 1,005 m³, similar to a Boeing 747.

paragraphs.heading: How it is built
paragraphs.text: The ISS is a modular station with two main halves. Roscosmos developed the Russian Orbital Segment, while NASA, ESA, JAXA and CSA built the US Orbital Segment. A frame called the Integrated Truss Structure links its solar panels and radiators to 16 large pressurized modules, which hold labs, living space, storage, controls and airlocks. Counting everything, the station has 43 modules and elements, plus eight ports where visiting craft can attach. Crews arrive on Soyuz and Crew Dragon, and once came on the Space Shuttle, while cargo comes on craft such as Progress, Cargo Dragon and Cygnus.

paragraphs.heading: Built by cooperation
paragraphs.text: The station is a political result of countries learning to work together in space during the space age. It merged two stations that had been planned separately: the Soviet Union's Mir-2 and America's Space Station Freedom. The first module went up in 1998, and big pieces were carried by Proton, Soyuz and Space Shuttle launch vehicles. The Expedition 1 crew arrived on 2 November 2000, and people have lived aboard ever since, the longest continuous human stay in space. By August 2025, 290 people from 26 countries had visited.

paragraphs.heading: Doing science there
paragraphs.text: The ISS gives experiments power, data links, cooling and a crew to tend them. Small uncrewed spacecraft can host some experiments too, but a station offers a long-term home where studies can run potentially for decades, with researchers close at hand. Groups of experiments can share one launch and the same crew time, which makes each one simpler. Work spans fields such as astrobiology, astronomy, materials science, space weather and space medicine, and scientists on the ground get the data quickly and can ask the crew to change a test. A crew of six gives about 160 hours of work a week, though looking after the station itself takes a good share of that.

paragraphs.heading: Hunting dark matter
paragraphs.text: One well-known experiment is the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer, or AMS, built to look for dark matter and to probe other basic questions about the universe. NASA rates it as important as the Hubble Space Telescope. It is mounted on the station because its needs for power and data would have been hard to meet on a satellite flying on its own. In April 2013 scientists reported that the AMS may have caught hints of dark matter: an unexplained surplus of high-energy positrons among the cosmic rays reaching Earth.

paragraphs.heading: What comes next
paragraphs.text: At least one more module is planned, the Payload Power Thermal Module from Axiom Space, which will form a commercial segment. The station is expected to keep working until the end of 2030, when parts of it are to become Axiom Station and the Russian Orbital Station. After that, the plan is to bring it down out of orbit with the US Deorbit Vehicle. That plan has drawn criticism, and a proposal to park the station in a higher, steadier orbit had gained support in Congress as of 2026.
